paragraphs.context: Let’s pretend the glass has got all soft like gauze
paragraphs.mainIdea: Alice imagines Looking-glass House and pretends the glass is soft. Then the glass really begins to melt like mist.
paragraphs.simple: Alice asks the kitten if it would like to live in Looking-glass House. She wonders if they would give it milk there, and she thinks that Looking-glass milk may not be good to drink. Then she talks about the passage. If you leave the door of their drawing room wide open, you can see a little of the passage in Looking-glass House. It is very like their passage as far as you can see, but it may be quite different further on. She says how nice it would be to get through into the house, and she is sure it has beautiful things in it. She says, let us pretend there is a way to get through, and that the glass has gone soft like gauze. Then she says the glass is turning into a sort of mist. She is up on the chimneypiece as she speaks, though she hardly knows how she got there. And the glass really is beginning to melt away, like a bright silver mist.

paragraphs.context: ’Twas brillig, and the slithy toves Did gyre and gimble in the wabe
paragraphs.mainIdea: This is the poem Jabberwocky. It has many made-up words. It tells how a boy kills a creature called the Jabberwock.
paragraphs.simple: The poem has many made-up words, so some of its parts are not clear. It begins with a scene that has strange creatures in it, and the creatures have made-up names. Then someone speaks to a boy, calling him "my son". He tells him to beware of the Jabberwock, which has jaws that bite and claws that catch. He also tells him to beware of the Jubjub bird and to keep away from the Bandersnatch. The boy takes his sword in his hand and looks for the enemy for a long time. He rests by the Tumtum tree and stands there for a while, thinking. While he stands there, the Jabberwock comes through the wood with eyes of flame, making noises as it comes. The boy hits it again and again with his sword and leaves it dead. He goes back with its head. Then the speaker asks if the boy has killed the Jabberwock and tells him to come to his arms. The speaker shouts glad words about the day and laughs in his joy. The poem ends with the same words that it began with.

paragraphs.context: if I don’t make haste I shall have to go back
paragraphs.mainIdea: Alice runs out of the room and floats down the stairs without touching them. She is glad to walk again in the usual way.
paragraphs.simple: Alice thinks that she must hurry, or she will have to go back through the Looking-glass before she has seen the rest of the house. She says she will look at the garden first. In a moment she is out of the room and goes down the stairs. At least it is not exactly running. It is a new way that she has invented for getting down the stairs quickly and easily. She keeps only the tips of her fingers on the handrail and floats gently down, and her feet do not touch the stairs. Then she floats through the hall. She would have gone straight out of the door in the same way, but she catches hold of the doorpost. She is getting a little giddy from so much floating in the air. She is rather glad to find herself walking again in the natural way.

paragraphs.context: I’ve heard nonsense, compared with which that would be as sensible as a dictionary
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Red Queen shakes her head. She says she has heard nonsense that was so much worse that this would seem as sensible as a dictionary.
paragraphs.simple: The Red Queen shook her head. She told Alice that she may call it nonsense if she likes. But the Queen said she had heard nonsense, and if you compare that nonsense with this, this would seem as sensible as a dictionary.

paragraphs.context: never changed their places at all: however fast they went
paragraphs.mainIdea: Alice and the Queen run fast, but the trees do not move past them. The Queen tells Alice not to talk.
paragraphs.simple: The strangest part was that the trees and the other things around them never changed their places. However fast they went, they never seemed to pass anything. Poor, puzzled Alice thought, "I wonder if all the things move along with us?" The Queen seemed to guess what she was thinking, and she cried, "Faster! Do not try to talk!"

paragraphs.context: it takes all the running you can do, to keep in the same place
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Red Queen says that in her country you must run as fast as you can just to stay in one place. To go somewhere else, you must run twice as fast.
paragraphs.simple: The Queen says it is a slow sort of country. She tells Alice that here you must do all the running you can just to stay in the same place. If you want to get somewhere else, you must run at least twice as fast as that.

paragraphs.context: they all thought in chorus (I hope you understand what thinking in chorus means
paragraphs.mainIdea: The voices in the train carriage think as a group that Alice should say nothing. They say that language costs a lot of money.
paragraphs.simple: Alice thought to herself, "Then there is no use in speaking." This time the voices did not join in, because she had not spoken. But to her great surprise they all thought together, like a chorus. The writer says he hopes you understand what thinking in chorus means, but he must say that he does not. They thought, "It is better to say nothing at all. Language is worth a thousand pounds a word!"

paragraphs.context: only think how convenient it would be if you could manage to go home without it
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Gnat says it would be easy for Alice to lose her name. Then the governess could not call her to lessons.
paragraphs.simple: The Gnat went on in a careless voice. He said that he did not know, and told Alice to think how easy it would be if she could go home without her name. For example, if the governess wanted to call Alice to her lessons, she would call out "come here" and then she would have to stop, because there would be no name for her to call. Then, of course, Alice would not have to go.

paragraphs.context: This must be the wood,” she said thoughtfully to herself, “where things have no names
paragraphs.mainIdea: Alice thinks about losing her name in the wood where things have no names. She thinks it would be funny but also a little bad.
paragraphs.simple: Alice says this must be the wood where things have no names. She wonders what will happen to her own name when she goes in. She would not like to lose it, because they would have to give her another, and it would almost surely be an ugly one. But then the fun would be in trying to find the creature that has her old name. She says it is like the notices when people lose dogs, which say that the dog answers to the name of Dash and had on a brass collar. She says to think of calling everything you met Alice until one of them answered. But she says they would not answer at all, if they were wise.

paragraphs.context: if it was so, it might be; and if it were so, it would be
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tweedledee answers with the opposite idea. He says what would be if it were so, and says it is not so. He calls this logic.
paragraphs.simple: Tweedledee said, on the other side, that if it was so, it might be, and if it were so, it would be. But as it is not so, it is not. He said that is logic.

paragraphs.context: But answer came there none — And that was scarcely odd, because
paragraphs.mainIdea: This is the last part of the poem. The Carpenter asks the oysters to go home, but no oyster answers, because they have all been eaten.
paragraphs.simple: The Carpenter said, "O Oysters, you have had a pleasant run! Shall we be trotting home again?" But no answer came. That was hardly strange, because the Walrus and the Carpenter had eaten every one.

paragraphs.context: “If that there King was to wake,” added Tweedledum, “you’d go out —bang!
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tweedledum says that Alice would disappear like a candle if the Red King woke up.
paragraphs.simple: Tweedledum added that if the King woke, Alice would go out with a bang, just like a candle.

paragraphs.context: The rule is, jam tomorrow and jam yesterday —but never jam today
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Queen says there is jam on the day before and the day after, but never on the day you are in.
paragraphs.simple: The Queen said that Alice could not have jam even if she wanted it. She said the rule is jam tomorrow and jam yesterday, but never jam today.

paragraphs.context: things that happened the week after next
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Queen remembers things that have not happened yet. She talks about a messenger who is punished before his trial.
paragraphs.simple: The Queen answered in a careless voice that she remembers things that happened the week after next. For example, she said, and she stuck a large piece of plaster on her finger as she spoke, the King's Messenger is in prison now, being punished. His trial does not even begin until next Wednesday. And of course the crime comes last of all.

paragraphs.context: sometimes I’ve believed as many as six impossible things before breakfast
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Queen says that she has had a lot of practice at believing impossible things.
paragraphs.simple: The Queen said she supposed Alice had not had much practice. She said that when she was Alice's age, she always did it for half an hour a day. She said that sometimes she had believed as many as six impossible things before breakfast. Then she cried that there goes the shawl again.

paragraphs.context: it means just what I choose it to mean
paragraphs.mainIdea: Humpty Dumpty says a word means just what he chooses it to mean, no more and no less.
paragraphs.simple: Humpty Dumpty said, in a rather scornful voice, that when he uses a word, it means exactly what he chooses it to mean. It does not mean more than that or less than that.

paragraphs.context: ‘slithy’ means ‘lithe and slimy.’ ‘Lithe’ is the same as ‘active.’
paragraphs.mainIdea: Humpty Dumpty explains the made-up word "slithy". He says it is like a portmanteau, with two meanings in one word.
paragraphs.simple: Humpty Dumpty said that "slithy" means "lithe and slimy". He said that "lithe" is the same as "active". He told Alice that it is like a portmanteau, because there are two meanings packed up into one word.

paragraphs.context: a ‘rath’ is a sort of green pig: but ‘mome’ I’m not certain about
paragraphs.mainIdea: Humpty Dumpty says what a rath is. He is not sure what "mome" means, but he gives his best idea.
paragraphs.simple: Humpty Dumpty said that a rath is a sort of green pig. He said he was not certain about "mome". He thought it was short for "from home", which would mean that they had lost their way.

paragraphs.context: To be able to see Nobody! And at that distance, too!
paragraphs.mainIdea: The King speaks as if Nobody were a person that Alice can see. He says his own eyes are not so good.
paragraphs.simple: The King said in an unhappy voice that he only wished he had such eyes: to be able to see Nobody, and from so far away! He said that it was as much as he could do to see real people by this light.

paragraphs.context: So of course Nobody walks slower than you
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Messenger says he passed Nobody on the road. The King takes "Nobody" to be a person who walks slower than the Messenger.
paragraphs.simple: The King said that was quite right, because the young lady had seen him too. So, he said, of course Nobody walks slower than the Messenger does.

paragraphs.context: First you take an upright stick,” said the Knight
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Knight describes his plan to stop hair falling off. You make your hair grow up a stick, because things never fall upwards.
paragraphs.simple: The Knight said that first you take a stick that stands straight up. Then you make your hair creep up it, like a fruit tree. He said the reason hair falls off is that it hangs down, and things never fall upwards. He said it is a plan of his own invention, and Alice may try it if she likes.

paragraphs.context: The only difficulty is with the feet: the head is high enough already
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Knight tells how he planned to get over a gate. He would put his head on the gate and stand on his head.
paragraphs.simple: The Knight said he would tell Alice how he came to think of it. He said he told himself that the only difficulty is with the feet, because the head is high enough already. So first he puts his head on the top of the gate. Then he stands on his head, and then the feet are high enough. Then he is over.

paragraphs.context: I don’t believe that pudding ever was cooked
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Knight says he does not think his new pudding was ever cooked, or will be. He still thinks it was a clever pudding to invent.
paragraphs.simple: The Knight said again that it was not the next day. He said that, in fact, and he held his head down and his voice got lower and lower, he did not believe that the pudding ever was cooked. He did not believe it ever would be cooked. And yet, he said, it was a very clever pudding to invent.

paragraphs.context: The bone wouldn’t remain, of course, if I took it
paragraphs.mainIdea: Alice answers the sum about taking a bone from a dog. She says the bone, the dog and she herself would not remain.
paragraphs.simple: Alice thought about it. She said that of course the bone would not remain if she took it. The dog would not remain either, because it would come to bite her. And she was sure that she would not remain!

paragraphs.context: we mostly have days and nights two or three at a time
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Red Queen says that in her country days and nights come together, and people join nights for warmth.
paragraphs.simple: The Red Queen said that Alice's way of having one day at a time is a poor, thin way of doing things. She said that here they mostly have days and nights two or three at a time. Sometimes in the winter they take as many as five nights together, for warmth.

paragraphs.context: it isn’t etiquette to cut anyone you’ve been introduced to
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Red Queen says it is not polite to cut someone you have met. The waiters take the leg of mutton away and bring a pudding.
paragraphs.simple: The Red Queen said very firmly, "Certainly not." She said that it is not proper behaviour to cut anyone you have been introduced to. She told the waiters to take the joint away. They carried it off and brought a large plum-pudding in its place.

paragraphs.context: shook her backwards and forwards with all her might
paragraphs.mainIdea: Alice takes the Red Queen off the table and shakes her hard.
paragraphs.simple: Alice took the Queen off the table as she spoke. She shook her one way and then the other, as hard as she could.

paragraphs.context: The Red Queen made no resistance whatever
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Red Queen does not try to stop Alice shaking her. She grows smaller, fatter, softer and rounder.
paragraphs.simple: The Red Queen did not try to stop her at all. Only her face grew very small, and her eyes got large and green. And Alice went on shaking her, and she kept on growing shorter, fatter, softer and rounder, and ...

paragraphs.context: whatever you say to them, they always purr
paragraphs.mainIdea: Alice thinks it is a bad habit of kittens that they always purr, whatever you say. This stops a conversation.
paragraphs.simple: Alice had once said that it is a very inconvenient habit of kittens that they always purr, whatever you say to them. She had said that if they would only purr for "yes" and mew for "no", or have any rule of that sort, one could keep up a conversation. But how can you talk with a person if they always say the same thing?

paragraphs.context: it must have been either me or the Red King
paragraphs.mainIdea: Alice asks Kitty to think who dreamed it all. She decides it was either herself or the Red King, and that each was part of the other's dream.
paragraphs.simple: Alice said to Kitty, "Let us think about who it was that dreamed it all." She said it is a serious question, and Kitty should not go on licking her paw, as if Dinah had not washed her that morning. She said it must have been either Alice or the Red King. He was part of her dream, but then she was part of his dream, too. She asked if it was the Red King, and said Kitty was his wife, so she ought to know. She asked Kitty to help to settle it, and said her paw could wait. But the annoying kitten only began on the other paw and pretended it had not heard the question.

sentences.context: that the white kitten had had nothing to do with it
sentences.simple: The white kitten was not part of it at all.
sentences.grammar: "had had" is the past perfect of "have": "had" is the helper and "had" is the main verb. "Have nothing to do with" means to have no part in something.

sentences.context: the ball of worsted Alice had been trying to wind up
sentences.simple: the ball of wool thread that Alice had been trying to wind up
sentences.grammar: "Alice had been trying..." is a relative clause with "that" left out: "the ball of worsted (that) Alice had been trying to wind up". It uses the past perfect continuous.

sentences.context: Suppose they had saved up all my punishments
sentences.simple: Think what would happen if they had kept all my punishments for later.
sentences.grammar: "Suppose + past perfect" means "What if...?" Alice asks about something that did not happen.

sentences.context: you never can tell, you know, unless our fire smokes
sentences.simple: You cannot know, unless our fire makes smoke.
sentences.grammar: "Unless" means "if not". "You never can tell" means that nobody can know.

sentences.context: I might have won, if it hadn’t been for that nasty Knight
sentences.simple: Perhaps I would have won, but the nasty Knight stopped me.
sentences.grammar: "If it hadn't been for X" means "without X". "Might have won" says it was possible, but it did not happen.

sentences.context: that she mightn’t take his breath away
sentences.simple: so that she would not take his breath away
sentences.grammar: "that she mightn't" means "so that she might not". It tells the purpose of lifting him slowly.

sentences.context: if I could get to the top of that hill
sentences.simple: I would see the garden much better if I could get to the top of that hill.
sentences.grammar: "if I could get..." talks about something Alice cannot do now. "I should see" tells what would happen if she could.

sentences.context: I could show you hills, in comparison with which you’d call that a valley
sentences.simple: I know of hills that are so high that you would call this one a valley.
sentences.grammar: "in comparison with which" means "when you put it next to them". "Which" stands for "hills" and joins this part to the word "hills".

sentences.context: I’ve heard nonsense, compared with which that would be as sensible as a dictionary
sentences.simple: I have heard nonsense that was so much worse that this would seem as sensible as a dictionary.
sentences.grammar: "compared with which" means "when you put it next to that". "Which" stands for "nonsense" and joins this part to the word "nonsense".

sentences.context: it takes all the running you can do, to keep in the same place
sentences.simple: You must run as much as you can, just to stay where you are.
sentences.grammar: "all the running you can do" means "as much running as you can do". "To keep in the same place" is an infinitive of purpose, meaning "in order to stay".

sentences.context: something about ‘horse’ and ‘hoarse,’ you know
sentences.simple: You could make a joke about the words "horse" and "hoarse", you know.
sentences.grammar: Wordplay: "horse" and "hoarse" are spelled differently but sound the same. Just before, the voice was hoarse, and Alice thought it sounded like a horse.

sentences.context: if the governess wanted to call you to your lessons
sentences.simple: For example, if the teacher wanted to call you to your lessons
sentences.grammar: "If + past tense" ("wanted") with "would" in the next part ("she would call out") is a conditional that talks about something that is only imagined.

sentences.context: the governess would never think of excusing me lessons for that
sentences.simple: The teacher would never think of letting me miss lessons because of that.
sentences.grammar: "excuse me lessons" means "let me off lessons": the verb "excuse" has two objects, "me" and "lessons".

sentences.context: of course you’d miss your lessons
sentences.simple: Of course, you would not go to your lessons.
sentences.grammar: Wordplay: "Miss" (the word the governess calls) and "miss" (to not go to something) sound the same. The Gnat then says, "That's a joke."

sentences.context: Waxworks weren’t made to be looked at for nothing, nohow!
sentences.simple: People did not make waxworks so that you could look at them without paying.
sentences.grammar: "for nothing" means "without paying". "Nohow" is a non-standard word for "not at all", so the sentence has a double negative, with "weren't" and "nohow".

sentences.context: if it were so, it would be; but as it isn’t, it ain’t
sentences.simple: If it were so, it would be so. But because it is not so, it is not.
sentences.grammar: "If it were so, it would be" is a conditional with "were" for an unreal idea. "Ain't" is a spoken short form of "isn't".

sentences.context: so that the Carpenter couldn’t count how many he took
sentences.simple: He did this so that the Carpenter could not count the number he took.
sentences.grammar: "so that" begins a clause of purpose. It says why the Walrus held his handkerchief in front.

sentences.context: If I wasn’t real,” Alice said —half-laughing through her tears
sentences.simple: Alice said, half laughing through her tears: if I were not real, I would not be able to cry.
sentences.grammar: "If I wasn't real" is an idea that is not true: Alice says she is real. The main part comes after the words "Alice said": "I shouldn't be able to cry".

sentences.context: shouldn’t have minded it so much,” said Tweedledum, “if it hadn’t been
sentences.simple: I would not have minded so much if it had not been a new one.
sentences.grammar: "shouldn't have minded... if it hadn't been" is a past conditional: it talks about something that did not happen in the past. "Hadn't been" means "had not been".

sentences.context: Well, yes, if you call that a-dressing
sentences.simple: Yes, if you want to call that "a-dressing".
sentences.grammar: Wordplay: Alice said "addressing" (speaking to someone), but the Queen hears "a-dressing", which sounds the same. Her next words are about dressing herself.

sentences.context: You couldn’t have it if you did want it
sentences.simple: You could not have it even if you wanted it.
sentences.grammar: "if you did want it": "did" is a stress word that makes "want" stronger. "Couldn't have" here means you would not be allowed to have it.

sentences.context: there’s one great advantage in it, that one’s memory works both ways
sentences.simple: There is one big good point: a person's memory works forwards and backwards.
sentences.grammar: "One's" means "a person's" and is a formal way to talk about people in general. The "that" clause tells what the advantage is.

sentences.context: it wouldn’t be all the better his being punished
sentences.simple: It would not be better if he were punished.
sentences.grammar: "his being punished" is a phrase with a possessive ("his") before an "-ing" word. It means "that he is punished". "All the better" means "even better".

sentences.context: The egg seems to get further away the more I walk towards it
sentences.simple: The more I walk towards the egg, the further away it seems to get.
sentences.grammar: "the more I walk" means "as I walk more". Two things change together: more walking, more distance.

sentences.context: If I’d meant that, I’d have said it
sentences.simple: If I had meant that, I would have said it.
sentences.grammar: "I'd" is short for "I had" in the first part and "I would" in the second. It is a past conditional about something that did not happen.

sentences.context: One can’t, perhaps,” said Humpty Dumpty, “but two can
sentences.simple: One person cannot, perhaps, but two people can.
sentences.grammar: "but two can" leaves out words, as "but two can help it". Humpty Dumpty means that with help from another person you could have left off at seven.

sentences.context: it means just what I choose it to mean
sentences.simple: It means exactly the thing that I choose it to mean.
sentences.grammar: "just what I choose it to mean" is a noun clause: "what" means "the thing which". "Neither more nor less" follows and means exactly that.

sentences.context: I only wish I had such eyes,” the King remarked
sentences.simple: I wish I had such eyes, but I do not.
sentences.grammar: "wish + past tense" ("had") talks about something that is not true now.

sentences.context: You might as well try to stop a Bandersnatch
sentences.simple: Trying to stop a minute is as hopeless as trying to stop a Bandersnatch.
sentences.grammar: "You might as well try to..." says that something is as hopeless as the thing named. Here the King says that stopping a minute is as hard as stopping a Bandersnatch.

sentences.context: it’s as well to be provided for everything
sentences.simple: It is wise to be ready for everything.
sentences.grammar: "it's as well to" means "it is wise to". "Provided for" means "made ready for".

sentences.context: To guard against the bites of sharks
sentences.simple: They are to keep the horse safe from shark bites.
sentences.grammar: This is an infinitive of purpose with no subject. It answers Alice's question "What are they for?" and "guard against" means "keep safe from".

sentences.context: the more head downwards I am, the more I keep inventing new things
sentences.simple: When my head is lower, I think of more new things.
sentences.grammar: "the more..., the more..." shows that two things grow together: more upside down, more new things.

sentences.context: I was as fast as —as lightning, you know
sentences.simple: I was as fast as lightning, you know. Here "fast" means held in place, not quick.
sentences.grammar: Wordplay on "fast": it can mean held in place, or very quick. The Knight was stuck in the helmet, but "as fast as lightning" usually means very quick. Alice says it is a different kind of fastness.

sentences.context: That’s what the name is called. The name really is ‘The Aged Aged Man.’
sentences.simple: That is what the name is called. The name itself is "The Aged Aged Man".
sentences.grammar: The Knight separates "what the name is called" from "what the name really is". The song has four different names in this part.

sentences.context: And the sooner we begin it, the better
sentences.simple: If we begin sooner, it will be better.
sentences.grammar: "the sooner..., the better" is a pattern with "the" and a word like "sooner" or "better". It shows that two things change together: sooner is better.

sentences.context: What do you suppose is the use of a child without any meaning
sentences.simple: What use do you think a child is without any meaning?
sentences.grammar: "do you suppose" is put into the question "What is the use of...?". After it, the word order is like a statement: "is the use", with no "does".

sentences.context: I said you couldn’t if you tried
sentences.simple: I said that you could not deny it, even if you tried.
sentences.grammar: "you couldn't" leaves out "deny it", which comes from the sentence before. The Red Queen answers Alice's "I don't deny things with my hands".

sentences.context: I speaks English, doesn’t I?
sentences.simple: I speak English, do I not?
sentences.grammar: The Frog uses non-standard grammar: "I speaks" and "doesn't I" use the third-person verb forms with "I". The standard forms are "I speak" and "don't I".

sentences.context: I’ll shake you into a kitten, that I will
sentences.simple: I will shake you until you are a kitten, I really will.
sentences.grammar: "that I will" is added at the end for emphasis: it repeats "I will" to show that Alice means what she says.

sentences.context: it must have been either me or the Red King
sentences.simple: I am sure it was either me or the Red King.
sentences.grammar: "must have been" shows that Alice is sure about something in the past. "Either... or" gives two possible answers.

make haste.meaning: To hurry; to do something quickly.
make haste.example: if I don’t make haste I shall have to go back

make out.meaning: To see or understand something with some effort. Here, to find out what a thing is.
make out.example: to make out what it could possibly be

leave off.example: it snowed so, they had to leave off

wind up.meaning: To wind thread round and round into a ball.
wind up.example: the ball of worsted Alice had been trying to wind up

catch up.meaning: To pick up quickly. Here, Alice takes the kitten up in her hands.

make up one's mind.example: she made up her mind to go on

set out.meaning: To start a trip or a walk.
set out.example: she set out once more down the path

take one's breath away.meaning: To surprise someone so much that they cannot speak for a moment.
take one's breath away.example: it quite seemed to take her breath away

get on.meaning: To do something and make progress. Here, "didn't get on very fast" means she did not make much progress.
get on.example: But she didn’t get on very fast

come undone.meaning: To open or come loose; to stop being tied or wound.
come undone.example: till it had all come undone again

get in the way.meaning: To be in the place where someone wants to go, so that they cannot pass easily.
get in the way.example: such a house for getting in the way

keep up with.meaning: To go as fast as someone else, so as not to fall behind.
keep up with.example: it was all she could do to keep up with her

in vain.example: Alice knocked and rang in vain for a long time

all the better.meaning: Even better. It adds more to the idea that something is good.
all the better.example: That would be all the better, wouldn’t it?

give up.meaning: To stop trying, because it is too hard.
give up.example: Alice sighed and gave it up

have any hand in.example: have had any hand in the mischief

to and fro.meaning: Moving one way and then back again.
to and fro.example: Who rocked his body to and fro

in time.meaning: After some time; when enough time has gone by.
in time.example: I shall be able to manage it quite well in time

no use.meaning: Not helpful; there is no good in doing it.
no use.example: It’s no use talking about it

on purpose.meaning: Not by chance; meaning to do it.
on purpose.example: almost as if it happened on purpose

come off.meaning: To come away from the place where it was fixed.

beg one's pardon.meaning: A polite way to say "Please say that again" or "I am sorry".

for fear of.meaning: Because you are afraid that something bad will happen.
for fear of.example: in a whisper, for fear of frightening them

I declare.meaning: A way to say strongly that something is true, often when you are surprised.
I declare.example: it’s turning into a sort of mist now, I declare!

out of breath.meaning: Breathing very fast after running, so that it is hard to speak.
out of breath.example: she was getting so much out of breath

turn out.meaning: To point outwards, away from each other.
turn out.example: turn out your toes as you walk

hold one's tongue.meaning: To keep quiet; to say nothing.
hold one's tongue.example: If you don’t hold your tongues, I’ll pick you!

all the same.example: My mind goes on working all the same

by the way.meaning: A way to add a new thing that you remember while talking.
by the way.example: By the way, Kitty, if only you’d been really with me

take hold of.meaning: To take something in your hand and keep it there.
take hold of.example: she took hold of the end of the pencil

set off.meaning: To start a trip or to begin to go.

take turns.meaning: To do something one after the other, in order.
take turns.example: if they really were to take turns in choosing subjects

find fault with.meaning: To say that someone or something is bad or has done wrong.
find fault with.example: ready to find fault with anybody

catch a crab.meaning: In rowing, to get the oar stuck in the water by mistake. Here the Sheep says Alice will do this.
catch a crab.example: You’ll be catching a crab directly

make believe.meaning: To pretend; to act as if something is true.
make believe.example: then you can make believe it’s oysters

look on.example: Alice looked on with great interest

break off.example: here she broke off with a frown
